Paragraph:
Translation: O descendant of Bharata, he who dwells in the body is eternal and can never be slain. Therefore you need not grieve for any creature.

Purport (Excerpt): The Lord now concludes the chapter of instruction on the immutable spirit soul. In describing the immortal soul in various ways, Lord Krsna establishes that the soul is immortal and the body is temporary... Therefore Arjuna as a ksatriya should not abandon his duty out of fear that his grandfather and teacher... will die in the battle.
Situation/Problem_Faced: Arjuna needs a definitive conclusion to the entire metaphysical discussion regarding life, death, and the soul to move forward.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: Krishna summarizes the previous verses into one conclusive rule: The indweller (soul) is eternal; the body is temporary; therefore, grief for *any* physical creature is unwarranted.
Outcome/Resolution: Krishna establishes the final philosophical baseline. The argument regarding the immortality of the soul is closed, setting the stage for the next phase of instruction regarding Arjuna's specific duty.

Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.cognitive Consolidation: Summarizing key learnings to form a solid belief

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Dehi (The embodied soul, the owner of the body)
Sarvabhuta (All creatures/beings; applying this truth universally)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: This verse acts as the concluding summary of Sankhya philosophy (analytical study of the body and soul) in this section. The absolute invulnerability of the 'dehi' (embodied soul) is the ultimate reason why a warrior of duty must conquer sentimental grief for any living being.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: This is a cognitive consolidation. After exploring various angles (metaphors, atheistic views, cosmic cycles), Krishna distills the entire complex discussion into a simple, memorable mantra. By synthesizing the teachings into a single, undeniable conclusion, he provides Arjuna with a clean cognitive slate, ending the rumination on death.
